questions.title: Context transition in a calculated column
questions.prompt: A calculated column on a Customer table classifies each customer as 'High' or 'Low' value by calling CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey])) and comparing it to 2500. Explain how this can possibly work, given that a calculated column only ever sees row context.
questions.modelAnswer: This works because of context transition: whenever CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside row context, DAX converts that row context into an equivalent filter context, restricted to just that row's values. For one specific customer row, the row context (this one CustomerKey) becomes a filter context, as if the whole model had been filtered down to just that customer. ALLEXCEPT(Customer, Customer[CustomerKey]) then removes any other filters on the Customer table while deliberately keeping the filter context transition just created on CustomerKey. SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) now sums only that one customer's sales, because the filter context -- via the relationship between Customer and Sales -- has narrowed the Sales table down to just their rows. Every row in the Customer table repeats this independently, one customer at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is exactly the kind of formula that looks impossible until you know about context transition, so I'd walk through it row by row. DAX is evaluating this calculated column for one specific customer at a time -- that's row context, nothing more. The moment CALCULATE appears inside that row context, DAX triggers context transition: it takes 'the row I'm currently on' and converts it into 'a filter restricting everything to just this row's CustomerKey.' ALLEXCEPT then does cleanup -- it strips any other filters that might be hanging around on the Customer table, while specifically preserving that CustomerKey filter context transition just created. So by the time SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) runs, the filter context has narrowed the related Sales table down to exactly one customer's transactions, through the relationship between the two tables. The IF then just compares that number to 2500. Nothing exotic is happening -- it's the standard shape of 'row context triggers CALCULATE triggers filter context,' which explains a whole category of DAX formulas that otherwise look like they're reading another table's data from inside row context by magic.
questions.example:
Customer Segment =
IF (
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( Sales[SalesAmount] ),
        ALLEXCEPT ( Customer, Customer[CustomerKey] )
    ) < 2500,
    "Low", "High"
)
-- CALCULATE triggers context transition: the current row's CustomerKey
-- becomes a one-value filter context, letting SUM reach into the related Sales table.
commonMistakes: Thinking a calculated column can never reference another table's aggregated data, missing that context transition is exactly what makes it possible
Forgetting that context transition happens automatically for an implicit CALCULATE wrapped around any measure reference, too
Misexplaining ALLEXCEPT as removing the CustomerKey filter instead of preserving it while removing everything else
Not recognizing the trigger condition precisely: CALCULATE evaluated inside row context
keyPoints: Context transition converts the current row context into an equivalent one-row filter context
It's triggered whenever CALCULATE evaluates an expression inside row context
A measure reference inside row context triggers it automatically too, via an implicit CALCULATE
ALLEXCEPT keeps the context-transition filter while removing other filters on the same table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines context transition and its trigger condition
Correctly walks through what happens for one customer row in this formula
Correctly explains ALLEXCEPT's role in preserving the context transition

questions.title: A measure is ignoring the report's slicer selections
questions.prompt: A measure called 'West Region Sales' was written as CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), Geography[Region] = "West"). When a user applies a slicer on Geography[State] set to multiple East Coast states, the measure still shows West region totals instead of narrowing further. Explain why, and how you'd fix it if the intent is for the measure to respect both the hardcoded region condition and the slicer together.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a column mismatch, not a CALCULATE overwrite problem in the way it first appears -- the measure filters Geography[Region], while the slicer filters Geography[State], a different column entirely, so there's nothing for CALCULATE to overwrite; the measure's filter on Region and the slicer's filter on State both remain active simultaneously, and the combination (West region AND East Coast states) likely returns an empty or near-empty result, which can look like the measure is 'ignoring' the slicer when it's actually honoring an impossible intersection. The real fix depends on intent: if Region and State should interact at all, the model likely needs the measure's logic reconsidered -- for instance, if the actual intent was ever for CALCULATE to override a same-column filter, KEEPFILTERS would make a new filter combine with (intersect) an existing one on the same column instead of overwriting it, but that only applies when both filters target the same column, which isn't the case here. The practical fix is recognizing the filters are on different columns and adjusting the DAX to filter on the column that's actually meant to interact with the slicer, or removing the hardcoded Region condition if State should be the only filter that matters.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether the measure's filter and the slicer's filter are even on the same column, because that's the detail that changes the whole diagnosis. Here they're not -- the measure hardcodes Geography[Region] = "West", and the slicer is on Geography[State]. CALCULATE's overwrite-by-default behavior only kicks in when a new filter targets a column that's already filtered; since Region and State are different columns, both filters stay active at the same time, which means the measure is actually doing exactly what it's coded to do -- show West region sales, further restricted to whichever East Coast states happen to also be in the West region (probably none, hence a confusing near-empty or unexpected result). This is a case where I'd go back to the business requirement rather than reach for KEEPFILTERS, because KEEPFILTERS solves same-column conflicts, and this isn't one. If the real intent was for the slicer to be the only thing controlling region/state filtering, I'd remove the hardcoded Region condition from the measure entirely rather than trying to patch the filter interaction.
questions.example:
-- The problem: two different columns filtered simultaneously, not a same-column overwrite
West Region Sales = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]), Geography[Region] = "West")
-- Slicer filters Geography[State] (East Coast states) -- a different column,
-- so both filters stay active together, likely producing an empty intersection.

-- If the true intent is for the slicer alone to control the result:
Region Sales = SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]) -- no hardcoded CALCULATE filter at all
commonMistakes: Assuming the measure 'isn't respecting' the slicer because of CALCULATE's overwrite behavior, when the real issue is two different columns both staying active
Reaching for KEEPFILTERS as a fix without checking whether the two filters even target the same column
Not recognizing that an unexpected near-empty result can be the system behaving correctly against a flawed assumption
Fixing the symptom by changing the slicer instead of questioning whether the hardcoded Region filter belongs in the measure at all
keyPoints: CALCULATE's overwrite-vs-combine behavior only applies to filters on the same column
A measure filtering one column and a slicer filtering a different column both stay active together
An unexpected result can mean the filters are correctly combining into an impossible intersection
The fix should match actual business intent, not just reflexively apply KEEPFILTERS or REMOVEFILTERS

Correctly explains why this isn't a CALCULATE overwrite scenario
Proposes a fix grounded in actual business intent rather than a reflexive KEEPFILTERS/REMOVEFILTERS patch

questions.title: Using USERELATIONSHIP for a role-playing date dimension
questions.prompt: Your model has one Date table related to a Sales fact table three ways -- Order Date, Ship Date, and Due Date -- but only the Order Date relationship is active by default. Write a measure that sums sales by Ship Date instead.
questions.modelAnswer: Only one relationship between two tables can be active by default, so with three date relationships on the same Sales table, only Order Date is active unless a measure explicitly reaches for another one. USERELATIONSHIP, used as a CALCULATE filter argument, activates a specific normally-inactive relationship for just that one calculation -- it doesn't change which relationship is active model-wide, only for the expression it's wrapped around.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the standard role-playing dimension pattern -- one Date table, several relationships to the same fact table, but only one of them can be the 'default' active relationship. For Ship Date sales, I wrap the plain SUM in CALCULATE and pass USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDateKey], 'Date'[DateKey]) as the filter argument. That tells DAX, for this one measure only, to use the Ship Date relationship instead of whichever one is active by default -- it doesn't touch the model's actual active/inactive relationship settings, it just reaches past them for this specific calculation. I'd build a parallel measure for Due Date the same way if needed, each one activating its own relationship, while a plain Total Sales measure continues to use the Order Date relationship since that's the one marked active.
questions.example:
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
    SUM(Sales[SalesAmount]),
    USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDateKey], 'Date'[DateKey])
)
-- Activates the Ship Date relationship for this one calculation only;
-- the model's actual active relationship (Order Date) is untouched.

Forgetting USERELATIONSHIP must be passed as a CALCULATE filter argument, not called on its own
Mixing up which table/column pair to pass -- it must match the actual inactive relationship's two columns
Assuming USERELATIONSHIP changes the relationship permanently rather than just for the one calculation
keyPoints: Only one relationship between two tables can be active by default
USERELATIONSHIP activates a specific inactive relationship for one calculation only
It's always used as a CALCULATE filter argument
This is the standard mechanism behind role-playing dimensions

questions.title: Deciding between an active and an inactive relationship
questions.prompt: You're modeling a Sales fact table with three date roles (Order, Ship, Due) all relating to one Date table. Only one relationship can be active by default. How do you decide which one to make active, and how do you handle the other two in your measures?
questions.modelAnswer: Since only one relationship between the Date table and Sales can be active, the design decision is to make active whichever date role most reports will filter and slice by default without extra configuration -- typically Order Date, since most sales analysis (trends, totals, year-over-year) is naturally anchored to when the order was placed. The other two relationships (Ship Date, Due Date) are created as inactive relationships, and any measure that specifically needs to report by Ship Date or Due Date uses USERELATIONSHIP inside a CALCULATE to activate the relevant one just for that calculation. This keeps the default, unqualified experience (dragging Date onto a visual with no special measure) working correctly for the most common case, while still supporting the less common date roles through dedicated measures rather than duplicating the Date table three times.
questions.professionalAnswer: The decision I'd make is: pick whichever date role is the default lens most people will actually use day to day, and that's almost always Order Date for a sales model -- most trend analysis, most 'how are we doing this quarter' questions, are implicitly about when the order happened. That one gets the active relationship, so a plain visual with Date on one axis and a Sales measure on the other just works with no special DAX. Ship Date and Due Date become inactive relationships to the same Date table -- I don't duplicate the Date table three times just to get three active relationships, because that fragments the model and breaks time-intelligence functions that expect one canonical date table. Instead, I write dedicated measures for the less common cases -- Sales by Ship Date, Sales by Due Date -- each using CALCULATE with USERELATIONSHIP to reach past the default. That gives report builders the simple default behavior for the common case, and explicit, discoverable measures for the specific cases, without duplicating the model.

Forgetting that only one relationship between two tables can be active, and trying to activate more than one

questions.title: Star schema or snowflake for the product hierarchy?
questions.prompt: You're designing a warehouse where the product hierarchy (Product -> Subcategory -> Category) is large and slowly changing. Explain the tradeoff between a star schema and a snowflake schema for this dimension, and give one concrete reason you might snowflake it anyway even though Microsoft's default guidance favors denormalization.
questions.modelAnswer: A star schema denormalizes the product hierarchy into one flat Product dimension table, with category and subcategory names repeated in every row -- that redundancy keeps the dimension exactly one join away from the fact table, which is the entire performance case for the star shape, at the cost of more storage and a hierarchy that must live in columns of one table. A snowflake schema normalizes the hierarchy into Product, Subcategory, and Category tables, each referencing the one above it -- less redundant storage and a naturally split hierarchy, at the cost of more joins and generally slower query performance. Microsoft's own guidance defaults to denormalized star dimensions, but snowflaking is still the right call in specific situations: for instance, if a separate sales-target fact table is stored at the subcategory grain while the main sales fact table is stored at the product grain, both need to join to the right level of the same hierarchy -- a snowflaked Subcategory table gives both fact tables a clean join target at their own grain, which a single flat Product table can't offer as cleanly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as a tradeoff between query-time joins and storage/maintenance, because that's really what's at stake. Star schema wins on query performance -- one join to reach any attribute, full stop, which is why Microsoft's own dimensional modeling guidance defaults to denormalized dimensions. Snowflake wins when the dimension is large enough that the redundant storage actually matters, or -- and this is the reason I'd actually reach for it here -- when I have two fact tables living at different grains within the same hierarchy. If my main sales fact table is at the product level but I also have a sales-target fact table at the subcategory level, I need a clean join target at the subcategory grain specifically. A single flat Product dimension doesn't give me that cleanly; a snowflaked Subcategory table does. In practice, I'd often split the difference: keep the ETL and storage layer normalized for maintainability, but expose a denormalized view to the reporting layer so Power BI still gets the one-join performance benefit without me paying the storage cost of a fully flattened table during the load.
commonMistakes: Treating snowflake vs. star as a different table classification rather than a normalization choice for dimensions specifically
Not identifying a concrete business reason to snowflake, only repeating the generic storage-savings tradeoff
Missing the multi-grain-fact-table scenario, which is the strongest practical reason to snowflake
Assuming Microsoft's guidance means star is always correct, missing the specific exceptions it calls out
keyPoints: Star schema: fully denormalized dimensions, fewer joins, faster queries, more storage

questions.title: The mechanics of SCD Type 2
questions.prompt: Explain exactly what happens to the data when a Type 2 slowly changing dimension attribute is updated -- for example, when a salesperson is reassigned from one sales region to another. Why does Type 2 require a surrogate key?
questions.modelAnswer: A Type 2 change is two operations, in order: first, UPDATE the existing row -- its EndDate (or ExpirationDate) is set to the date the change took effect, and its IsCurrent flag flips from TRUE to FALSE, permanently preserving it as history. Second, INSERT a brand-new row with a new surrogate key (never reused), the same natural key (it's still the same salesperson), the new attribute value (the new sales region), a StartDate equal to the old row's EndDate, and IsCurrent set to TRUE. There are now two rows for the same salesperson -- that's the entire point. A new surrogate key is required because the natural key is now duplicated across two rows; if dimension rows were identified only by their natural key, the warehouse couldn't tell which version a given fact should join to. The surrogate key makes each version uniquely addressable: fact rows loaded before the change point to the old surrogate key, fact rows loaded after point to the new one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as two statements that together represent one business event. First, I update the existing row -- not delete it -- setting its EndDate to when the change happened and flipping IsCurrent to false, so it becomes permanent, closed-out history. Second, I insert a brand-new row for the same salesperson, same natural key, but a new surrogate key, the new region, a StartDate that picks up exactly where the old row's EndDate left off, and IsCurrent set to true. Both of these should run as one transaction, since they represent a single logical event. The reason the surrogate key is non-negotiable here: once I have two rows sharing the same natural key, I need something else to disambiguate them, and that's exactly what the surrogate key is for -- fact rows loaded before the reassignment keep pointing at the old surrogate key, and anything loaded after points at the new one, so historical reports naturally show the right region for sales that happened under the old assignment.
questions.example:
UPDATE DimSalesperson
SET    ExpirationDate = '2024-05-23',
       IsCurrentFlag   = 0
WHERE  SalespersonKey = 296;

INSERT INTO DimSalesperson
  (BusinessKey, SalesRegionKey, EffectiveDate, ExpirationDate, IsCurrentFlag)
VALUES (758596752, 5, '2024-05-23', '9999-12-31', 1);
-- Both statements represent one business event and should run in a single transaction.
commonMistakes: Describing Type 2 as deleting the old row instead of updating it and preserving it as history
Forgetting the new row needs a brand-new surrogate key, not a reused or regenerated one
Not explaining why the natural key alone is insufficient once two versions exist
Running the UPDATE and INSERT as two unrelated statements instead of one transaction representing one business event
keyPoints: Type 2 change = UPDATE the old row (close it out) + INSERT a new versioned row
The old row's EndDate/IsCurrent gets set; it's preserved, never deleted
The new row gets a brand-new surrogate key, same natural key, new attribute value
A surrogate key is required because the natural key becomes duplicated across versions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the UPDATE step (closing out the old row)
Correctly describes the INSERT step (new version, new surrogate key)
Correctly explains why a surrogate key is required

questions.title: Writing the SCD Type 2 UPDATE and INSERT pair
questions.prompt: An employee (BusinessKey 112233, current surrogate key 58) moves from DepartmentKey 3 to DepartmentKey 7 on 2025-02-14. Write the UPDATE and INSERT statements that correctly apply this as a Type 2 change against a DimEmployee table with columns EmployeeKey, BusinessKey, DepartmentKey, EffectiveDate, ExpirationDate, and IsCurrentFlag.
questions.modelAnswer: The existing row (EmployeeKey 58) must be updated to close it out: set ExpirationDate to the change date and IsCurrentFlag to 0. A new row must be inserted with the same BusinessKey (112233), the new DepartmentKey (7), an EffectiveDate equal to the old row's new ExpirationDate (2025-02-14), a far-future ExpirationDate (e.g. 9999-12-31) marking it as the open-ended current version, and IsCurrentFlag set to 1. The new row gets a new surrogate EmployeeKey, generated automatically (e.g. via IDENTITY) rather than reused from the old row.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as the standard two-statement Type 2 pattern, both representing one business event. First, close out the existing row -- EmployeeKey 58 -- by setting its ExpirationDate to 2025-02-14 and flipping IsCurrentFlag to 0. Second, insert the new version: same BusinessKey since it's still the same person, the new DepartmentKey of 7, EffectiveDate starting exactly where the old row's ExpirationDate ended, a far-future ExpirationDate like 9999-12-31 to mark it as the current open-ended version, and IsCurrentFlag set to 1. I'd let the new EmployeeKey come from an IDENTITY column rather than picking a number myself, since surrogate keys should never be reused or manually assigned. I'd also wrap both statements in a transaction, since they represent one atomic business event -- the reassignment -- and shouldn't ever be allowed to apply only halfway.

Manually assigning a new surrogate key instead of letting an IDENTITY column generate it
Forgetting to flip IsCurrentFlag to 0 on the old row, leaving two rows both marked current
Running the UPDATE and INSERT outside a transaction, risking a half-applied change

The new row's EffectiveDate matches the old row's new ExpirationDate exactly
The new row gets IsCurrentFlag = 1 and a far-future ExpirationDate
Both statements should run as one transaction representing one business event

questions.title: When to consolidate flags into a junk dimension
questions.prompt: Your sales fact table has accumulated eight separate one-off flag dimensions: order status, payment method, rush-order flag, gift-wrap flag, and four others, each with two or three rows. Explain what a junk dimension is, how it's built, and when consolidating these flags into one would be the wrong move.
questions.modelAnswer: A junk dimension is a single dimension table that consolidates several small, unrelated, low-cardinality attributes into one table in place of many separate ones -- a deliberate catch-all for miscellaneous flags, not a designed business entity. It's built mechanically as the Cartesian product of every value in every attribute being combined, with one surrogate key column identifying each unique combination: two attributes with three values each produce nine rows, one per combination. After consolidation, the fact table's eight foreign keys collapse into one, narrowing the fact table and reducing the join count for any report filtering on those flags. Good candidates share three traits: many of them, few attributes each (often just one column), and low cardinality. It would be the wrong move if any of the eight attributes has real, independent business meaning that analysts need to filter or slice on their own terms (that belongs in a real dimension, not junked), or if the combined cardinality would explode -- eight attributes with even modest value counts each can multiply out to a number of rows larger than anything that's actually useful, at which point the junk dimension becomes worse than what it replaced.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first confirm these eight really are junk-dimension candidates and not just under-designed real dimensions -- the tell is low cardinality, few columns each, and no independent business meaning on their own. Order status, payment method, and the rush/gift-wrap flags fit that profile well. Mechanically, I'd build the junk dimension as the Cartesian product of every combination across the attributes being combined -- if I combine, say, order status (3 values) and delivery status (3 values), I get nine rows, one surrogate key per combination. That replaces two foreign keys on the fact table with one, which both narrows the fact table and simplifies the field list for anyone browsing the model in Power BI. Where I'd stop and push back: if combining all eight attributes together would multiply out to tens of thousands of rows, that's a sign the combined cardinality has grown too large and the junk dimension has become counterproductive -- at that point, I'd either junk a smaller subset of the truly low-cardinality flags together and leave the rest as their own dimensions, or reconsider whether a couple of these 'flags' are actually business entities people want to filter by in their own right, which would disqualify them from being junked at all.
commonMistakes: Consolidating an attribute with genuine independent business meaning into the junk dimension, making it harder for analysts to filter on it directly
Not recognizing that the row count grows multiplicatively (Cartesian product), not additively, as more attributes are combined
Junking a single flag on its own instead of reserving the technique for consolidating many small ones
Missing that this is specifically a fact-table-narrowing technique -- it reduces foreign keys, not just the number of dimension tables
keyPoints: A junk dimension consolidates several small, unrelated, low-cardinality attributes into one table
It's built as the Cartesian product of every combination of the consolidated attributes' values
Good candidates: many of them, few attributes each, low cardinality
Wrong to junk an attribute with independent business meaning, or when combined cardinality explodes

questions.title: Modeling a many-to-many relationship with a bridge table
questions.prompt: A sale can legitimately be credited to two or three salespeople who worked the deal together, and any one salesperson is credited on many sales. Design how you'd model this relationship between the Sale fact table and the Salesperson dimension, and explain why the table you build to resolve it is itself a factless fact table.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a genuine many-to-many relationship -- no amount of clever fact-table design turns it into a clean one-to-many, because a sale really can have multiple salespeople and a salesperson really is credited on multiple sales. The fix is a bridge table (also called a join table): instead of one foreign key on the Sale fact table pointing straight at the Salesperson dimension, the fact relates to a 'Sale Salesperson' bridge table storing one row per valid sale-salesperson combination, and the bridge table relates to the Salesperson dimension -- two clean one-to-many relationships standing in for the one many-to-many relationship. For a sale split three ways, the bridge table gets three rows, each pointing at the same SaleID and a different SalespersonID. The bridge table is itself a factless fact table because it contains nothing but foreign keys -- SaleID and SalespersonID, no measures to sum -- so a row only records that an association happened; the only thing it supports is a count of rows, which is the exact definition of a factless fact table.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recognize up front that this relationship is genuinely many-to-many, not a modeling mistake to be designed away -- some sales really do get split across multiple salespeople. The standard resolution is a bridge table sitting between the Sale fact and the Salesperson dimension: instead of the fact table pointing directly at Salesperson, it points at a 'Sale Salesperson' bridge table, which in turn points at Salesperson. That turns one many-to-many relationship into two clean one-to-many relationships, which is something both the warehouse and Power BI's relationship model can actually represent cleanly. Concretely, if a sale is split three ways, the bridge table gets three rows for that one SaleID, each with a different SalespersonID. The thing I'd call out unprompted, because it's a detail that signals real understanding: look at what columns that bridge table actually has -- just the two foreign keys, nothing to sum or average. That makes it a factless fact table by definition -- it records that an association occurred, and the only measurement it supports is literally counting rows, which is exactly what you'd use it for if someone asked 'how many salespeople were involved in this sale' or 'how many sales did this person touch.'
commonMistakes: Trying to force a one-to-many relationship by picking just one 'primary' salesperson per sale, losing real information
Adding measure columns to the bridge table, missing that a factless fact table by definition has none
Not recognizing the bridge table resolves the many-to-many into two one-to-many relationships, describing it vaguely instead
Forgetting that a three-way split sale produces three separate bridge rows, not one row with three salesperson columns
keyPoints: Some relationships are genuinely many-to-many and can't be modeled as one-to-many
A bridge table resolves this into two clean one-to-many relationships
One row per valid combination (e.g. three rows for a three-way split sale)
A bridge table with only foreign keys is a factless fact table -- countable, not summable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies this as a genuine many-to-many relationship
Correctly designs the bridge table and its two one-to-many relationships
Correctly describes the row-per-combination behavior for a split sale
Correctly explains why the bridge table is a factless fact table

questions.title: Sales totals doubled after adding a salesperson bridge table
questions.prompt: After introducing a Sale-Salesperson bridge table to correctly model multiple salespeople per sale, the total sales amount shown in a Power BI report is now higher than the actual total revenue. Diagnose why, and explain how you'd fix the measure.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a classic fan-out trap: once the Sale fact table is related (even indirectly, through the bridge table) to a table where one sale can appear multiple times -- once per credited salesperson -- any measure that sums SalesAmount through that relationship path double- or triple-counts sales that were split across multiple salespeople, because the filter context now matches multiple bridge rows per sale. A sale split three ways gets its SalesAmount counted three times once the bridge table's relationships are in the picture, inflating the total. The fix is to make sure the core Total Sales measure aggregates at the fact table's own grain, independent of the bridge table relationship -- for example, by ensuring the measure doesn't inadvertently traverse the bridge table's one-to-many direction when computing a grand total, or by using a measure that explicitly sums distinct sales (e.g. via a FILTER or a dedicated 'total revenue' measure built directly off the Sale fact table without passing through the bridge), while a separate 'sales by salesperson' measure is expected to show the split amounts per salesperson and isn't the one being used for a grand total.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the fan-out trap, and it's almost always the first thing that goes wrong the moment a bridge table enters a model. The mechanism is straightforward once you see it: a sale split across three salespeople now has three rows in the bridge table pointing back at the same SaleID. If a 'Total Sales' measure's filter context flows through that bridge table relationship -- say, because the report visual includes a Salesperson field alongside the total -- SQL Server (or the VertiPaq engine) effectively counts that one sale's SalesAmount three times, once per bridge row. The totals aren't actually wrong in isolation -- summing by salesperson is correct, each salesperson really is credited with that sale -- but a report-wide grand total that flows through the same path inflates. The fix is to keep a dedicated grand-total measure that's computed at the Sale fact table's own grain and doesn't traverse the bridge table at all, so overall revenue is always counted once per sale regardless of how many salespeople it's split across, while the per-salesperson breakdown measure is understood to legitimately double-count at the summary level by design.
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is wrong (duplicate fact rows) instead of recognizing the fan-out happens through the relationship, not the underlying fact table
Trying to fix it by deduplicating the fact table, which would break the legitimate per-salesperson breakdown
Not recognizing this is the same fan-out risk inherent to any bridge table or many-to-many relationship
Fixing the per-salesperson measure instead of recognizing the grand-total measure is the one that needs to avoid the bridge table path
keyPoints: A bridge table legitimately creates multiple rows per sale when it's split across salespeople
Any measure whose filter context flows through the bridge table double-counts split sales
A per-salesperson breakdown correctly counts each sale once per credited person -- that's by design
A grand-total measure needs to be computed at the fact table's own grain, independent of the bridge table

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the fan-out / double-counting mechanism caused by the bridge table
Correctly distinguishes the legitimate per-salesperson count from the inflated grand total
Proposes a correct fix for the grand-total measure

questions.title: Presenting the full Microsoft BI stack to stakeholders
questions.prompt: You built a capstone project moving raw data through SQL Server, into a warehouse via SSIS, then out through both an SSRS paginated report and a Power BI dashboard connected to the same warehouse. Tell me how you'd present this architecture to a hiring manager who wants to understand not just what you built, but why you made the design choices you did.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer walks through the pipeline end to end in plain language and justifies each tool choice by the problem it solves: SQL Server holds the raw/staging data because it's the reliable system of record; SSIS handles the ETL because it can run on a schedule, handle incremental loads, and recover from partial failures via checkpoints rather than requiring a full reload every time; the warehouse is modeled as facts and dimensions (star schema) specifically so both downstream tools can query it efficiently without each one reinventing its own data shape; SSRS serves the paginated, fixed-layout reporting need (something that prints predictably and matches a line-item format); Power BI serves the interactive, self-service exploration need. The key point to make explicit: connecting both SSRS and Power BI to the same warehouse, rather than each tool having its own separate extract, means the two tools can never disagree with each other -- a single source of truth was a deliberate design decision, not an accident.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk a hiring manager through it as a story with a reason behind every tool, not just a list of technologies. Raw data lands in SQL Server because I need a reliable, transactional place to stage it. SSIS does the heavy lifting of moving and reshaping that data into the warehouse -- and I'd specifically mention the incremental load design and the checkpoint-based restartability, because that shows I was thinking about what happens when something fails at 2am, not just the happy path. The warehouse itself is a star schema, which I'd justify by saying it keeps both downstream tools fast and simple to query, since neither SSRS nor Power BI has to do the modeling work themselves. Then the split at the end -- SSRS for the fixed, printable paginated report and Power BI for the interactive dashboard -- I'd frame as matching the tool to the actual use case rather than picking a favorite: some stakeholders need something that prints exactly the same way every time, others need to slice and explore. And the detail I'd make sure lands: both of those report tools point at the same warehouse, not separate copies of the data, specifically so nobody ever has to ask 'why does the Power BI number not match the SSRS number' -- that's a single source of truth, and it was a deliberate decision, not a coincidence.
commonMistakes: Listing the tools used without explaining why each one was chosen for its specific role
Not mentioning the deliberate single-source-of-truth decision (both tools hitting the same warehouse)
Describing only the happy path, without mentioning error handling or incremental load design decisions
Being too technical/jargon-heavy for a hiring-manager-level explanation of 'why,' not just 'what'
keyPoints: Each tool choice (SQL Server, SSIS, warehouse, SSRS, Power BI) is tied to a specific reason
The warehouse's star schema design serves both downstream reporting tools efficiently
Connecting both report tools to the same warehouse was a deliberate single-source-of-truth decision
Mentions resilience design (incremental loads, checkpoints) as evidence of production-mindedness

Justifies each major tool choice with a specific reason

What went wrong, and how did you work through it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific, real integration snag rather than a vague generality -- for example, discovering that a report built against the warehouse's staging shape broke once the warehouse was properly modeled into facts and dimensions, or that SSRS and Power BI needed slightly different connection configurations (credentials, gateway, or query folding behavior) to hit the same warehouse cleanly. It explains the diagnostic process (comparing what each tool actually received versus expected, checking connection strings/permissions, verifying the underlying query), the fix applied, and -- just as important -- what was learned about designing for multiple consumers from the start next time, such as building the warehouse's reporting layer with both tools' needs in mind up front rather than retrofitting one after the other was already built.

questions.title: EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks
questions.prompt: You need to find every customer who has placed at least one order. Compare writing this with EXISTS, with IN, and with an INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT. Explain how each one behaves when a customer has multiple orders, and the specific trap with NOT IN when the subquery's column can contain NULLs.
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS, IN, and INNER JOIN with DISTINCT can all answer 'does this customer have at least one order,' but they get there differently. EXISTS(subquery) is a pure existence check -- SQL Server can stop scanning the moment it finds one matching row, and a customer with ten orders still only produces one result row, because EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's rows, just a true/false per outer row. IN (subquery) compares the outer column against the whole list the subquery returns; it also naturally avoids duplication since it's testing membership, not joining. An INNER JOIN behaves differently: joining Customer to Order on CustomerID and a customer with three orders produces three joined rows, which means DISTINCT (or GROUP BY) is required afterward to get back to one row per customer -- without it, the result silently overcounts. The sharper trap is with NOT IN rather than IN: if the subquery's column can contain a NULL, NOT IN against that list returns no rows at all for every single outer row, because SQL's three-valued logic can never prove an inequality against an unknown value. EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it's testing a condition, not comparing against a value list, which is one reason NOT EXISTS is generally the safer choice for 'does not have a match.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why these three roads to the same destination aren't actually equivalent in practice. EXISTS is the one I reach for by default for a pure existence check -- it's a yes/no test, the optimizer can bail out the instant it finds one match, and a customer with ten orders still contributes exactly one row to the result, because EXISTS never pulls the subquery's actual data back. IN behaves similarly for this particular case -- it's checking membership in a list, not joining, so it also doesn't duplicate. Where people get burned is reaching for a plain INNER JOIN instead: the moment you join Customer to Order, a customer with three orders becomes three rows, and if you forget the DISTINCT, you've silently inflated your result set without an error anywhere to tell you. But the real gotcha I always bring up, because it's bitten people in production, is NOT IN with a nullable column -- if even one NULL sneaks into the subquery's result, NOT IN returns completely empty, for every row, with no warning. I treat that as a hard rule: never write NOT IN against a column that could contain NULL -- use NOT EXISTS instead, which doesn't have that failure mode at all.
questions.example:
-- EXISTS: pure existence check, no duplication risk
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM [Order] o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

-- IN: membership test against the subquery's result list
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o);

-- JOIN: requires DISTINCT or a customer with 3 orders appears 3 times
SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
INNER JOIN [Order] o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;

-- THE TRAP: if Order.CustomerID can be NULL, this returns ZERO rows for every customer:
SELECT c.CustomerID FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o); -- avoid if nullable
commonMistakes: Writing a plain INNER JOIN for an existence check and forgetting DISTINCT, silently duplicating customers with multiple orders
Using NOT IN against a subquery column that can contain NULL, not realizing it returns zero rows for every outer row
Assuming EXISTS and IN always perform identically to a JOIN, when EXISTS can short-circuit and avoid materializing the whole list
Not recognizing that EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's column values -- only whether a match exists
keyPoints: EXISTS is a short-circuiting existence check; it returns one result row regardless of how many matches exist
IN compares against a list but doesn't duplicate rows the way a JOIN does
An INNER JOIN needs DISTINCT/GROUP BY to avoid duplicating a row per matching child record
NOT IN against a nullable column can return zero rows entirely -- NOT EXISTS avoids that trap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EXISTS's existence-check, non-duplicating behavior
Correctly explains why a JOIN needs DISTINCT to avoid duplication
Correctly identifies the NOT IN / NULL trap and why NOT EXISTS avoids it

questions.title: Routing rows with a Conditional Split
questions.prompt: Describe how you'd configure an SSIS Conditional Split transformation to route incoming order rows into three outputs: 'High Value' (OrderTotal > 1000), 'Standard' (OrderTotal between 1 and 1000), and a catch-all for anything else, including negative or zero totals that shouldn't normally occur.
questions.modelAnswer: A Conditional Split evaluates its case expressions in order, top to bottom, and sends each row down the first case that evaluates to true -- so case order matters, and once a row matches one case it's done, it isn't also tested against the others. I'd define two named outputs plus rely on the built-in default output rather than defining three explicit cases: 'High Value' with the condition OrderTotal > 1000, and 'Standard' with the condition OrderTotal > 0 && OrderTotal <= 1000. Everything that doesn't match either named case -- specifically zero, negative totals, or NULLs -- falls through to the Conditional Split's default output, which I'd rename to something explicit like 'Unexpected Total' rather than leaving it as the generic default, and route that to an error-staging table or a flat file for investigation rather than silently discarding it. The key design point is that the default output isn't optional cleanup -- it's actually where the unexpected and invalid rows a real source system will eventually produce end up, so it needs a real downstream destination, not a dead end.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up with two explicit named cases and let the Conditional Split's built-in default output catch everything else, rather than trying to write a third explicit condition for it. First case, 'High Value': OrderTotal > 1000. Second case, 'Standard': OrderTotal > 0 && OrderTotal <= 1000. The order of the cases matters here -- the transformation tests top to bottom and a row goes down the first match, so I'd double check 'High Value' is listed first since it's the more specific, higher bound. Anything that doesn't match either -- zero, negative, or NULL OrderTotal, which shouldn't happen but absolutely will eventually in a real feed -- falls into the default output. I always rename that default output to something like 'Unexpected Total' instead of leaving the generic label, and I never leave it unconnected -- I route it to a staging table or a log file specifically so a data-quality problem shows up as rows I can go look at, rather than vanishing silently out of the pipeline.

-- Conceptual SSIS Conditional Split configuration (not T-SQL):
-- Output 1 'High Value'  : OrderTotal > 1000
-- Output 2 'Standard'     : OrderTotal > 0 && OrderTotal <= 1000
-- Default output (renamed 'Unexpected Total'): everything else -- zero, negative, NULL
-- Route the default output to an error-staging table, not a dead end.

Ordering the 'Standard' case before 'High Value', causing high-value rows to incorrectly match the broader condition first
Leaving the default output unconnected, silently dropping rows with unexpected or invalid totals
Forgetting that a row is evaluated against cases top to bottom and only goes down the first match, not every matching case

The built-in default output catches anything that matches no explicit case -- no third condition needed
Case order matters when conditions could overlap (place the more specific/bounded case first)
The default output should be renamed and routed somewhere real, never left as a dead end

Correctly relies on the default output instead of a redundant third case
Correctly explains case evaluation order and why it matters here
